title: How Microglia Let a Touch Through

scenes.tts: After a nerve injury, a light touch can make a rat pull away. What changed in the spinal cord, and who changed it?
scenes.visual: Title card: How Microglia Let a Touch Through. A spinal cord cross-section with the dorsal horn highlighted. Question: what changed in the cord, and who changed it?
scenes.narration: After a nerve injury, a light touch can make a rat pull away. What changed in the spinal cord, and who changed it?

scenes.tts: Meet a lamina one neuron, in the outermost layer of the dorsal horn. It sends signals toward the brain.
scenes.caption: Meet a lamina I neuron, in the outermost layer of the dorsal horn. It sends signals toward the brain.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the dorsal horn: one neuron labelled lamina I neuron, with its axon heading up toward a brain outline.
scenes.narration: Meet a lamina I neuron, in the outermost layer of the dorsal horn. It sends signals toward the brain.

scenes.tts: In a simple picture, a light touch excites it a little. Inhibitory synapses hold it below threshold.
scenes.visual: A voltage gauge beside the neuron with a dashed threshold line. A touch input nudges the needle up; an inhibitory synapse pulls it back below the line. Corner label: simple picture.
scenes.narration: In a simple picture, a light touch excites it a little. Inhibitory synapses hold it below threshold.

scenes.tts: Those synapses open channels that pass chloride. They pull the voltage toward the anion reversal potential.
scenes.visual: The inhibitory synapse opens a channel; chloride ions flow. A marker on the gauge labelled E_anion sits low.
scenes.narration: Those synapses open channels that pass chloride. They pull the voltage toward the anion reversal potential.

scenes.tts: That potential stays low because a transporter, K C C two, carries potassium and chloride out of the cell.
scenes.caption: That potential stays low because a transporter, KCC2, carries potassium and chloride out of the cell.
scenes.visual: A cotransporter in the membrane, labelled KCC2, carrying one potassium ion and one chloride ion out of the cell together. Drawn as a cotransporter, not a pump.
scenes.narration: That potential stays low because a transporter, KCC2, carries potassium and chloride out of the cell.

scenes.tts: In two thousand three, Coull, De Koninck and colleagues studied rats after nerve injury. Their lamina one neurons had less K C C two.
scenes.caption: In 2003, Coull, De Koninck and colleagues studied rats after nerve injury. Their lamina I neurons had less KCC2.
scenes.visual: The KCC2 cotransporter fades. Label: less KCC2; the anion gradient shifts. Credit: Coull, De Koninck and colleagues, 2003; rats after nerve injury.
scenes.narration: In 2003, Coull, De Koninck and colleagues studied rats after nerve injury. Their lamina I neurons had less KCC2.

scenes.tts: Their anion reversal potential had shifted up. That does not mean the neuron itself depolarized.
scenes.visual: The E_anion marker slides up the gauge toward the threshold line. A note: the reversal potential moved, not the neuron.
scenes.narration: Their anion reversal potential had shifted up. That does not mean the neuron itself depolarized.

scenes.tts: Predict. As that potential rises toward threshold, what happens to the inhibitory synapse's grip?
scenes.visual: The gauge with the E_anion marker partway up. Question on screen: what happens to inhibition's grip?
scenes.narration: Predict. As that potential rises toward threshold, what happens to the inhibitory synapse's grip?

scenes.tts: Recall the balance-point rule. The synapse can only pull the voltage toward its own reversal potential.
scenes.visual: Balance-point scale: leak, touch and inhibitory ropes pull a marker toward their reversal potentials. Label: steady state, no injected current; weights are conductances.
scenes.narration: Recall the balance-point rule. The synapse can only pull the voltage toward its own reversal potential.

scenes.tts: So as that potential rises, the pull weakens. Less excitation is needed to fire the cell.
scenes.visual: The inhibitory rope keeps its weight; only its anchor, E_anion, moves up. Label: same anion conductance, weaker pull near threshold. A bar shows the excitation needed to reach threshold shrinking.
scenes.narration: So as that potential rises, the pull weakens. Less excitation is needed to fire the cell.

scenes.tts: In a passive model with made-up values, this touch leaves the steady voltage below threshold in the healthy cell. With the reversal potential at minus fifty-five millivolts, it sits exactly at the threshold boundary. At minus fifty millivolts, it sits above it.
scenes.caption: In a passive model with made-up values, this touch leaves the steady voltage below threshold in the healthy cell. With the reversal potential at −55 mV, it sits exactly at the threshold boundary. At −50 mV, it sits above it.
scenes.visual: Table on screen, labelled illustrative passive model, steady voltages, not measurements. Values: leak 1 at −65 mV, inhibition 1, touch 0.4 toward 0 mV, threshold −50 mV. E_anion −70 mV: −56.2 mV, below threshold. −55 mV: −50.0 mV, at threshold. −50 mV: −47.9 mV, above threshold. Footnote on screen: equilibrium values; crossing threshold in time needs a sustained input.
scenes.narration: In a passive model with made-up values, this touch leaves the steady voltage below threshold in the healthy cell. With the reversal potential at −55 mV, it sits exactly at the threshold boundary. At −50 mV, it sits above it.

scenes.tts: Notice what did not happen. Inhibition did not have to turn into excitation. It only had to weaken.
scenes.visual: Two labels: crossed out, inhibition flips to excitation; kept, inhibition weakens. Small note: in this steady-state model; in real cells, timing and location also matter.
scenes.narration: Notice what did not happen. Inhibition did not have to turn into excitation. It only had to weaken.

scenes.tts: So what changed the neuron? Not a neuron.
scenes.visual: The neuron dims. A small branching cell appears beside it with a question mark.
scenes.narration: So what changed the neuron? Not a neuron.

scenes.tts: Tsuda and colleagues, in rats, found P two X four receptors on reactive microglia. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the cord.
scenes.caption: Tsuda and colleagues, in rats, found P2X4 receptors on reactive microglia. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the cord.
scenes.visual: A microglia cell with glowing receptors labelled P2X4. ATP droplets nearby. A neuron and an astrocyte drawn without the receptor. Label: Tsuda and colleagues, rats.
scenes.narration: Tsuda and colleagues, in rats, found P2X4 receptors on reactive microglia. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the cord.

scenes.tts: They ran two tests. Lowering P two X four suppressed the allodynia. So the receptor was needed.
scenes.caption: They ran two tests. Lowering P2X4 suppressed the allodynia. So the receptor was needed.
scenes.visual: Split panel, left: P2X4 lowered; the withdrawal-threshold curve rises back up. Label: the receptor was needed.
scenes.narration: They ran two tests. Lowering P2X4 suppressed the allodynia. So the receptor was needed.

scenes.tts: Microglia stimulated with A T P were transferred into rats never injured. Those rats developed allodynia. So stimulated microglia were enough.
scenes.caption: Microglia stimulated with ATP were transferred into rats never injured. Those rats developed allodynia. So stimulated microglia were enough.
scenes.visual: Split panel, right: ATP-stimulated microglia from a dish go into a naive rat; its threshold curve falls. Label: stimulated cells were enough.
scenes.narration: Microglia stimulated with ATP were transferred into rats never injured. Those rats developed allodynia. So stimulated microglia were enough.

scenes.tts: The messenger came in two thousand five. Coull and colleagues showed that stimulated microglia release B D N F.
scenes.caption: The messenger came in 2005. Coull and colleagues showed that stimulated microglia release BDNF.
scenes.visual: The microglia cell releases dots labelled BDNF toward the lamina I neuron. Label: Coull and colleagues, 2005, rats.
scenes.narration: The messenger came in 2005. Coull and colleagues showed that stimulated microglia release BDNF.

scenes.tts: B D N F acts through track B receptors. It shifts the anion reversal potential up, the same change seen after injury.
scenes.caption: BDNF acts through TrkB receptors. It shifts the anion reversal potential up, the same change seen after injury.
scenes.visual: BDNF binds TrkB receptors; the E_anion marker on the gauge slides up again.
scenes.narration: BDNF acts through TrkB receptors. It shifts the anion reversal potential up, the same change seen after injury.

scenes.tts: Block that signalling, and both the shift and the allodynia reverse.
scenes.visual: A block icon over TrkB. The E_anion marker drops back down, and the threshold curve rises.
scenes.narration: Block that signalling, and both the shift and the allodynia reverse.

scenes.tts: Three papers, different links, all in rats. The behavioural readout was always a withdrawal threshold. The last link, from weaker inhibition to a touch that fires, is a model.
scenes.visual: The completed chain in a row: injury, P2X4 in microglia, BDNF, TrkB, E_anion shift, weaker inhibition, then a dashed final link to a touch that fires, labelled model. Tags under the links: KCC2 and E_anion, Coull 2003; P2X4, Tsuda 2003; BDNF and TrkB, Coull 2005. Overall tags: rats; behavioural readout, withdrawal threshold.
scenes.narration: Three papers, different links, all in rats. The behavioural readout was always a withdrawal threshold. The last link, from weaker inhibition to a touch that fires, is a model.

scenes.tts: Now the twist. Sorge, Mapplebeck and colleagues gave male and female mice a nerve injury. The hypersensitivity was comparable.
scenes.visual: The chain shrinks to the top; male and female mouse icons appear. A grid starts to fill: rows male intact, female intact, female lacking adaptive immune cells. Label: Sorge, Mapplebeck and colleagues, mice.
scenes.narration: Now the twist. Sorge, Mapplebeck and colleagues gave male and female mice a nerve injury. The hypersensitivity was comparable.

scenes.tts: In males, a microglial inhibitor reversed the hypersensitivity. In females, under the conditions tested, it did not.
scenes.visual: Grid: male intact, yes. Female intact, no, under the conditions tested. Third row shows a question mark.
scenes.narration: In males, a microglial inhibitor reversed the hypersensitivity. In females, under the conditions tested, it did not.

scenes.tts: Predict. Intact females seemed to rely on adaptive immune cells. What does the inhibitor do in females lacking those cells?
scenes.visual: The third row of the grid pulses: female, lacking adaptive immune cells. Question mark.
scenes.narration: Predict. Intact females seemed to rely on adaptive immune cells. What does the inhibitor do in females lacking those cells?

scenes.tts: It works. The route can switch.
scenes.visual: Third row fills in: yes. A switch icon between microglia and adaptive immune cells.
scenes.narration: It works. The route can switch.

scenes.tts: A later study found the same pattern in rats. So it is not a quirk of mice, but it stays conditional.
scenes.visual: A rat icon joins the grid with the same male yes, female no pattern. Label: conditional on model and assay.
scenes.narration: A later study found the same pattern in rats. So it is not a quirk of mice, but it stays conditional.

scenes.tts: Macrophages in the dorsal root ganglion add another route. In mice, depleting macrophages throughout the body reduced hypersensitivity in both sexes. The authors favoured the ganglion macrophages, but skin dendritic cells were depleted too.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to the dorsal root ganglion; macrophages expand around sensory neurons. Labels: mice; systemic depletion; both sexes; skin dendritic cells also depleted.
scenes.narration: Macrophages in the dorsal root ganglion add another route. In mice, depleting macrophages throughout the body reduced hypersensitivity in both sexes. The authors favoured the ganglion macrophages, but skin dendritic cells were depleted too.

scenes.tts: So ask of any immune result: which cell, in which sex, in which compartment?
scenes.visual: Takeaway card with three questions: which cell? which sex? which compartment?
scenes.narration: So ask of any immune result: which cell, in which sex, in which compartment?
